A LITTLE HELP

Your guide to HeatSafe

Start with your city. Then explore the weather, the air and the hours ahead.

Get started in five steps

  1. Choose a city using the City menu below the logo and tabs.
  2. Choose a period. Use Last 12 hours, Last 7 days or Last 30 days. For your own dates, open Custom dates, click a start day, click an end day, then Apply range. Reset brings back the next 24/48 hours. Empty charts mean that period has no available records.
  3. Pick a tab at the top. Each tab explains a different part of the picture.
  4. Read a marker or tap a point on a chart to see a value and time. You can also use the keyboard to focus chart points.
  5. Ask the assistant at the bottom. Try “What was Karachi’s temperature on 23 September 2025?” Include the city and year for a precise lookup. You can ask a follow-up question.
What do the top numbers mean?

The strip below the tabs changes with the tab you open. Read the small label below each number to see its period.

Temperature
How warm the air is, in degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit.
Feels like / heat index
Temperature and humidity combined. Humid air can make heat feel stronger.
US AQI
An air-quality score. Higher numbers mean more polluted air. The category, such as Good or Moderate, gives quick context.
NO₂ and O₃
Nitrogen dioxide and ozone: gases in the air. Their readings show gas concentration, not particle mass or an AQI score.
Humidity
How much moisture is in the air, shown as a percentage.
Wind
How fast the wind is moving, in metres per second.
Peak, high and low
The largest or smallest available value in the selected period. These are different from the latest conditions.
Overview: understand the city at a glance

The main sentence combines the weather and air-quality outlook. The centre shows the latest source conditions. The smaller cards point out warmer and cooler times. Use Plan your hours or Explore the air to open the detail tabs.

The latest-conditions display stays at the latest source time even when you select historical dates. The period label tells you which outlook the summary uses.

Forecast: read the lines and prediction

The lines compare air temperature and calculated heat index. The vertical marker says where the prediction starts. The shaded area and dashed lines show future weather-model estimates. Solid lines on the left show recent model estimates where available.

Peak and low labels point to useful moments. The hourly bars compare how warm different hours may feel; a longer bar means warmer within that period.

The separate Stored ML card is one saved heat-index prediction from the project model. Check its target date and status. An out-of-date card is not a new prediction for today. Some cities have an outlook but no stored live ML prediction.

Air quality: understand the area and particle charts

The AQI area chart shows how the air-quality score changes over time. Higher points mean a higher pollution score. The coloured scale and category help you read the current score.

PM2.5 and PM10 are particle concentrations: how much particle mass is in a cubic metre of air. Higher lines mean more particles by mass. PM2.5 measures smaller particles; PM10 includes those smaller particles too. Do not add the two readings together. These values are not AQI scores.

The longer-view chart uses the stored historical archive: monthly averages by default, or daily averages for chosen dates. The floating dots are an illustration, not live particle measurements. A missing archive or empty period is labelled.

Network and Sources: follow the evidence

In Network, select a dot to see its value, date and source. Its connected lines light up. Drag the map to move it, use + and − to zoom, and use the legend to focus a group.

Sources & updates shows where the data comes from and how it refreshes. Model error is the model’s average past prediction error; lower is better. R² describes how well it explained variation in the historical test data. Test hours tells you how many historical hours were used for those scores. Neither score promises the next prediction will be exact.

Freshness, themes and the assistant

Last source pull at the top right is when the server fetched source data. It may differ from the time the conditions are valid for. Weather and air values are model estimates, not readings from sensors at your location.

The page checks for updates every five minutes while open. A source response can be reused for fifteen minutes. Stored database and ML results change when the project data is rebuilt and deployed.

Use the ◐ button to change colours. Beige/maroon is the default; your chosen theme is saved in your browser.

The assistant looks up the small amount of data needed for your question and replies in everyday language with sources. If a date or city has no records, it should tell you. Check source dates and ask it to explain uncertainty.
